title: The returning starter: permission, exposure and repeatability
subtitle: Guide a professional pitcher from throwing eligibility to a repeatable restricted role after UCL reconstruction.
role: Rehabilitation S&C coach working with the treating clinician, surgeon, athletic trainer and pitching coach

brief: Adrián is a fictional professional right-handed starter working through late rehabilitation after a documented UCL graft reconstruction. A muscle-splitting approach and associated ulnar-nerve procedure are recorded. He wants to return to a rotation role. The affiliate has an opening, and every good session creates pressure to accelerate.

You implement permitted physical preparation and reconcile the athlete’s response with the throwing plan. Clinical examination, diagnosis, treatment restrictions and medical clearance belong to the treating clinical team. Each checkpoint supplies the information available at that moment. Choose the next defensible action, then identify what evidence would justify a later change.

These are selected episodes across a longer course, not seven consecutive sessions or a complete rehabilitation protocol. Interim authorized work is omitted. All athlete details, throw counts, symptom ratings and staff instructions are synthetic teaching data. They are not recommended doses, validated limits or predictions of recovery.

athlete.Procedure: UCL tendon-graft reconstruction; muscle-splitting approach; associated ulnar-nerve procedure documented
athlete.Target role: Starter with planned preparation, between-inning work and repeat outings
athlete.Current context: Late rehabilitation; physical preparation continues within the signed plan
athlete.Authority: Treating clinician and surgeon govern clinical progression; pitching and performance staff implement and report

constraints: A prior surgeon instruction requires review before first throwing, first mound work, live hitters and competition. Passing a checkpoint here does not replace those sign-offs.

Current permitted gym work follows the rehabilitation clinician’s written exercise list. New high-speed arm exercises, weighted-ball drills and unplanned mound work need clarification; they are not automatically allowed.

The fictional team instruction is to stop the throwing task and contact the clinician for new medial elbow pain, tingling, altered sensation or loss of motion. Do not test through these findings or diagnose graft failure yourself.
Account separately for preparation throws, the planned task, between-inning throws and extras. A throw count describes exposure; it does not measure ligament force.
Record during-session, later-that-day and next-morning response. Missing follow-up is unknown, not a symptom-free result.

mnemonic.expansion: Permission → Exposure → Response → Function → Opportunity to repeat → Role → Medical handoff. Use it as a memory aid, not a clearance score.

checkpoints.title: 1. The calendar says ready; the permission does not
story: Adrián has completed his permitted strength and movement work without reported symptoms. The clinician records motion relative to his own documented throwing-arm baseline and acceptable capacity for review. The surgeon’s first-throw sign-off is still pending. A coach offers an easy catch session because the athlete has passed the anticipated calendar milestone.

observations.label: Clinical record
observations.value: Review requested; first throwing not signed
observations.interpretation: A proposed milestone and a completed examination are different records.

observations.label: Physical work
observations.value: Permitted tasks completed without reported symptoms
observations.interpretation: Encouraging evidence within those tasks; throwing has not been tested.

observations.label: Player comparison
observations.value: Teammate returned sooner after augmented repair
observations.interpretation: A different procedure and athlete do not alter this reconstruction plan.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What should you arrange today?

options.text: Start easy catch and ask for approval afterward.
options.feedback: Even low-intent catch introduces an unauthorized task. “Easy” is not a substitute for the requested surgical review.
options.consequence: The first throwing exposure would be undocumented progression beyond the current permission.

options.text: Send the readiness packet for sign-off and continue the already permitted training.
options.feedback: Correct. Summarize the examination, comparable capacity measures and response, and obtain the missing first-throw decision.
options.consequence: Training continues within scope while the clinical team sets a specific throwing task and monitoring plan.

options.text: Stop all physical preparation until he is cleared for games.
options.feedback: The case permits other work. A pending throwing decision does not automatically remove those permissions.
options.consequence: Useful permitted preparation would be lost without a supplied clinical reason.

checkpoints.rationale: The subsequent story assumes the clinical team reviews the packet and separately authorizes a specified flat-ground stage. Elapsed time still matters to the treating plan, but does not grant permission by itself.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Treating clinician coordinates first-throw authorization with the surgeon; S&C reports permitted task performance.
progressionEvidence: Explicit first-throw permission and task limits.
Clinical and comparable physical findings interpreted together.
Agreed observer, response checks and escalation contact.
stopOrReview: Missing sign-off.
Changed symptoms or motion before the authorized task.

checkpoints.title: 2. A clean session with an incomplete recovery record
story: Under the new written plan, Adrián completes 12 preparation throws and 18 task throws: 30 documented throws. He reports no medial symptoms during or later that day. He leaves early for a family commitment, and the next-morning response has not been recorded. Today’s draft advances both distance and intent.

observations.label: Actual exposure
observations.interpretation: Preparation is part of the record, even when the worksheet emphasizes task throws.

observations.label: Current response
observations.interpretation: A synthetic report of no symptoms at those checks; not proof of tissue capacity.

observations.label: Next morning
observations.interpretation: The planned response check is missing, not zero.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: Which response preserves useful progress without inventing evidence?

options.text: Advance both variables because the completed session was pain-free.
options.feedback: The next-morning check is part of this plan, and two proposed changes would make the next response harder to interpret.
options.consequence: The staff would progress with an incomplete record.

options.text: Repeat the previous session immediately without contacting the athlete.
options.feedback: Repeating is still an exposure. First obtain the missing response and confirm the permitted next task.
options.consequence: Even an unchanged dose could conflict with information not yet collected.

options.text: Obtain the follow-up and let the agreed plan determine whether to repeat or change a specified demand.
options.feedback: Correct. Ask about location, timing, sensation, motion and task tolerance; report the response before the next exposure.
options.consequence: The next task is based on completed observations rather than an assumed symptom-free morning.

checkpoints.rationale: A simple count needs context. The later record confirms no reported symptoms at the missing check; subsequent authorized flat-ground work is completed before mound review. No catch-up throws are added.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Athletic trainer or rehabilitation clinician collects and interprets the follow-up; performance staff reconciles the log.
progressionEvidence: Complete scheduled response checks.
Consistent task execution within the signed plan.
A named next task with its intended change and monitoring.
stopOrReview: New localized symptoms or altered sensation.
Unexplained missing work or recovery observations.

checkpoints.title: 3. Mound entry is a change of task
story: Following review, the clinician and surgeon authorize a controlled mound session under specified limits. The fictional plan contains 12 preparation throws and 24 mound throws, with the pitching coach controlling the task. Adrián asks to keep that count but add a harder finishing set and a new breaking-ball sequence.

observations.label: Written task
observations.interpretation: An authorized example for this player; not an entry-stage recommendation.

observations.label: Requested addition
observations.value: Same count; greater intent and changed pitch mix
observations.interpretation: A stable count does not mean an unchanged task.

observations.label: Recovery evidence
observations.interpretation: Supports review for mound entry; does not establish tolerance of every mound demand.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: How do you organize this first authorized mound task?

options.text: Deliver the signed session, document actual intent and pitch mix, and review before adding new demands.
options.feedback: Correct. Keep the planned task interpretable and report its execution and response.
options.consequence: The staff learns about the authorized mound exposure rather than an improvised package of changes.

options.text: Approve both additions because total count stays at 36.
options.feedback: Count cannot capture intent, pitch selection or task context. The additions are not within the supplied authorization.
options.consequence: The apparent matching count conceals a changed exposure.

options.text: Declare mound work successful as soon as one pitch matches his old velocity.
options.feedback: A single output does not establish response, command, repeatability or completion of the task.
options.consequence: The staff would mistake one performance observation for stage completion.

checkpoints.rationale: He completes the specified 36-throw session without reported symptoms. Record whether the intended task was actually delivered, then follow the existing recovery checks. Do not convert one symptom-free exposure into unrestricted throwing.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Pitching coach supervises the authorized task; clinical staff reviews response and stage changes.
progressionEvidence: Actual task matches permission.
Clinical response and comparable capacity information remain acceptable to the treating team.
Repeated authorized exposure is documented before broader role demands are proposed.
stopOrReview: Unplanned change in intent or pitch mix.
New symptoms, deteriorating execution or a request exceeding the signed plan.

checkpoints.title: 4. The extras matter, even when the pain settles
story: At a later scheduled session, the same 12 preparation and 24 task throws are planned. Adrián adds eight harder throws after the supervised set. Their velocities were not recorded. That evening he reports medial discomfort rated 3/10 and intermittent small-finger tingling. By morning the pain is absent, but the tingling occurred again while dressing.

observations.label: Actual exposure
observations.interpretation: Eight extras exceed the 36-throw plan; intensity is incompletely measured.

observations.label: Pain response
observations.interpretation: Improvement in pain does not erase the event or resolve the sensory complaint.

observations.label: Other evidence
observations.interpretation: Relevant history for clinician review, not a diagnosis of nerve injury or graft failure.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What is the immediate staff action?

options.text: Use a shorter bullpen as a test because morning pain is zero.
options.feedback: The case instruction is to stop and seek review for these findings. An improvised test bullpen is another exposure, not a clinical assessment.
options.consequence: An unresolved symptom change would be loaded without authorization.

options.text: Pause throwing, promptly send the full exposure and symptom record to the treating clinician, and obtain revised permissions.
options.feedback: Correct. Preserve timing, location, sensory details and missing intensity; do not label this structural failure yourself.
options.consequence: Clinical reassessment governs what resumes, while other work is limited to activities the team still permits.

options.text: Diagnose recurrent UCL tearing and remove him from all training indefinitely.
options.feedback: The findings warrant assessment, but this information cannot establish that diagnosis or an indefinite restriction.
options.consequence: A justified referral would be replaced by an unsupported conclusion.

checkpoints.rationale: The urgency here comes from a changed localized and sensory response under the fictional team instructions, not from crossing a universal 3/10 threshold. Clinical staff determines examination, further investigation and activity restrictions.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Treating clinician leads reassessment and communicates with the surgeon as indicated; staff records actual exposure.
progressionEvidence: Completed reassessment and a revised written plan.
Resolution or management of the findings to the clinician’s satisfaction.
A specifically authorized re-entry task and follow-up.
stopOrReview: Recurrent or persistent tingling, pain, swelling or loss of motion.
Any request to resume before the clinical decision.

checkpoints.title: 5. Re-entry earns evidence; it does not recover lost time
checkpoints.phase: Revised controlled work toward live hitters
story: After assessment and follow-up, the clinician permits a revised controlled task and records no current sensory complaint. The case does not disclose a diagnosis or imaging result, so do not invent one. The revised example includes 12 preparation and 20 task throws. Subsequent authorized sessions are completed as directed, with stable observations. A roster coordinator proposes skipping directly to a game to recover the lost schedule.

observations.label: Re-entry exposure
observations.interpretation: A fictional clinician-authorized revision, not a standard percentage reduction.

observations.label: Subsequent response
observations.value: No reported recurrence at specified checks
observations.interpretation: Useful serial observations after re-entry, not proof of zero future risk.

observations.label: Untested demand
observations.value: Live hitters and reactive inning context
observations.interpretation: These have not yet been demonstrated in the resumed pathway.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What should the staff propose next?

options.text: Ask for review of a bounded live-hitter task once the documented clinical and controlled-work criteria are met.
options.feedback: Correct. Define the new context, limits, observer and recovery checks before obtaining the required sign-off.
options.consequence: The next step tests a relevant missing demand without assuming game readiness.

options.text: Compress two stages into one day to make up the interrupted schedule.
options.feedback: Lost calendar time is not a dose prescription. The case supplies no permission for compressed exposure.
options.consequence: Schedule pressure would determine the progression.

options.text: Treat the lower throw count as evidence that reconstruction has failed.
options.feedback: A modified re-entry task is not a diagnostic result. The clinical team has authorized it after review.
options.consequence: The learner would turn a management decision into an unsupported diagnosis.

checkpoints.rationale: The team later grants a bounded live-hitter session. That is a new decision with explicit permission; the case does not claim that a certain number of good mound sessions automatically earns it.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Clinical team authorizes live progression; pitching and performance staff specify and monitor the task.
progressionEvidence: The revised plan has been completed as instructed.
Current clinical status and relevant function are reviewed.
The live task describes context, planned exposure, limits and recovery review.
stopOrReview: Any recurrence or unexplained change.
Requests to trade missed days for extra exposure.

checkpoints.title: 6. A hitter changes the problem
story: The signed live session contains 14 preparation, 30 live and six between-block throws: 50 total. Adrián has no reported symptoms at the scheduled checks. His command deteriorates in the last block, and he reports rushing between pitches when runners are introduced. His best velocity matches an old high point.

observations.label: Exposure accounting
observations.interpretation: The live count alone would omit 20 documented throws.

observations.label: Performance
observations.value: Peak velocity restored; late command and tempo inconsistent
observations.interpretation: A best pitch and sustained role execution answer different questions.

observations.label: Clinical response
observations.value: No reported symptoms at specified checks
observations.interpretation: Supports review; cannot independently establish unrestricted competitive readiness.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: How should the staff use this session?

options.text: Activate him without restrictions because his best pitch is back.
options.feedback: Peak velocity ignores task consistency, clinical authority and the demands of a starter role.
options.consequence: A narrow performance success would become an unsupported availability claim.

options.text: Interpret late command loss as proof of recurrent injury.
options.feedback: The observation has several possible explanations and requires context. No diagnosis follows from command alone.
options.consequence: Performance variability would be misclassified as a clinical finding.

options.text: Review the late-block limitation, refine permitted live work and seek a separately defined restricted-competition plan.
options.feedback: Correct. Present both the reassuring response and the unresolved execution demand.
options.consequence: The staff can decide what further rehearsal or bounded competition is appropriate, with explicit limits.

checkpoints.rationale: After additional authorized rehearsal and review, the treating team grants restricted competition. The limitation, response and role demands are documented rather than concealed by the best velocity.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Pitching staff interprets execution with the athlete; clinical staff grants or withholds competition permission.
progressionEvidence: An explicit restricted-competition decision.
Sufficiently repeatable task execution for that proposed role, as judged by the staff.
A plan for preparation, outing limits, recovery and the next review.
stopOrReview: Clinical symptom change.
Execution deterioration that requires reassessment of the permitted task.

checkpoints.title: 7. Two outings are evidence about two outings
checkpoints.phase: Return to performance and repeated availability
story: Adrián completes two restricted outings separated by the staff-prescribed recovery interval. Each has 16 preparation, 36 competitive and 10 between-inning throws: 62 documented throws. Clinical checks remain acceptable in the case, and command is more consistent. The club now asks him to become an unrestricted starter and also be available for unexpected short-rest relief. Neither additional demand has been authorized or rehearsed.

observations.label: Actual outings
observations.interpretation: Keep each outing and recovery interval visible; the sum is not a tissue-load measure.

observations.label: Demonstrated role
observations.value: Two bounded outings under a planned recovery pattern
observations.interpretation: This supports that specific pattern, not every possible availability schedule.

observations.label: Requested change
observations.interpretation: Workload and role uncertainty would both change.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What should the return-to-performance report conclude?

options.text: Continue the authorized role and request a coordinated review before expanding length or changing availability.
options.feedback: Correct. State what was demonstrated, what remains untested and who must authorize the next role.
options.consequence: The next performance goal is explicit while clinical and operational boundaries remain visible.

options.text: Declare rehabilitation complete with no further monitoring.
options.feedback: Repeated participation is valuable, but the case has not demonstrated the proposed unrestricted role.
options.consequence: The report would erase the remaining demand gap.

options.text: Add short-rest relief first because it involves fewer game pitches.
options.feedback: Fewer game pitches do not establish equivalent preparation, recovery or availability demands.
options.consequence: A different role would be introduced without the required review.

checkpoints.rationale: Return to performance is an ongoing evaluation of role execution and repeatable availability. A useful report can be positive about demonstrated progress while specific about the next untested demand.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Clinical and baseball leadership agree availability; performance and pitching staff report execution and recovery.
progressionEvidence: Explicit role and exposure permissions.
Repeated execution and recovery consistent with the proposed availability pattern.
Documented decision ownership, next goal and review event.
stopOrReview: A new role, shorter recovery or larger exposure outside the existing permission.
Recurrent symptoms or unexpected loss of function.

assignment.brief: Prepare a one-page return-to-role packet for the final staff meeting. Include the setback rather than reporting only the successful outings. Use the case facts; leave unspecified dates, examination details and velocities unknown.
deliverables: A procedure and permission summary separating reconstruction from repair.
An exposure ledger for the selected episodes, including warm-up, between-block and extra throws.
A setback handoff with symptom timing, sensory complaint and decision owner.
A three-column statement: demonstrated demands, untested demands, proposed next review.
A short athlete-facing explanation of why returning to games and returning to his full role are different decisions.
rubric: Correctly preserves procedure-specific restrictions and clinical ownership.
Accounts for 44 actual throws at the setback and 50 at the live session; does not convert missing velocity to zero.
Responds to the sensory complaint without diagnosing graft failure.
Separates peak velocity, role execution and repeatable availability.
Proposes a conditional next decision with evidence and ownership, not an invented clearance date.
modelResponse: Adrián has a documented graft reconstruction and associated nerve procedure. The team has authorized restricted competition after reassessment and staged work. The earlier setback followed 44 actual throws against 36 planned, including eight harder throws of unknown velocity; medial pain and intermittent small-finger tingling triggered clinical review. The later authorized re-entry and serial observations must be recorded without inventing the clinician’s undisclosed diagnosis.

The live session contained 50 total throws, including 20 outside live pitching. Peak velocity returned before command and tempo were repeatable. Two later restricted outings each contained 62 documented throws and were tolerated under their prescribed recovery pattern. This demonstrates progress within that pattern. It does not establish unrestricted starts or short-rest relief readiness.

Continue the presently authorized role. Request joint clinical and baseball review of the next proposed demand, specifying preparation, outing length, recovery, monitoring and staff ownership. Explain to Adrián that his successful outings count as meaningful evidence; the next job is to demonstrate and obtain permission for the particular role being requested.

recall.prompt: Hide the pathway. Explain PERFORM and name two reasons a symptom-free bullpen does not automatically authorize a game.
recall.answer: Permission, Exposure, Response, Function, Opportunity to repeat, Role, Medical handoff. A bullpen may omit live or repeat-availability demands, and competition still requires its own clinical authorization. Its count also may hide preparation or extra throws.

transfer.prompt: A different pitcher has a selected partial UCL injury treated nonoperatively. Which ideas transfer, and which case details must be replaced?
transfer.answer: Transfer explicit permission, complete exposure records, serial response, relevant task execution and role-specific review. Replace the graft and surgical restrictions with that athlete’s diagnosis, clinical findings, treatment plan and authorized progression. Neither a reconstruction calendar nor an augmented-repair example sets the nonoperative schedule; new symptoms still require clinical interpretation.

anatomy.title: Medial elbow: three relationships to remember
anatomy.caption: Conceptual native elbow load sharing: upper arm, forearm, medial restraint region and flexor–pronator support. The ulnar nerve is not drawn; its symptoms still matter in this case, and associated nerve surgery can alter its position. This is not a postoperative map or an attachment footprint.

demands.title: Each setting adds a question
demands.caption: Selected progression questions, not a calendar. Each setting requires its own permission and response review; the pathway may pause, repeat or return to an earlier authorized task.
demands.alt: Five-step demand map moving from flat ground to controlled mound, live hitters, restricted games and repeated role availability.

steps.label: Flat ground
steps.detail: Is the authorized task and recovery response documented?

steps.label: Controlled mound
steps.detail: Can the intended mound task be executed repeatedly?

steps.label: Live hitters
steps.detail: What changes with hitters, runners and inning rhythm?

steps.label: Restricted games
steps.detail: Can the permitted competitive task be completed?

steps.label: Repeat the role
steps.detail: Does execution and recovery support the specific availability pattern?

response.title: Count the work; keep the response separate
response.caption: Synthetic selected episodes, not consecutive sessions or a dose schedule. Exposure means documented throws; response is the maximum reported medial elbow discomfort at the episode’s specified checks, on a 0–10 scale. The setback also included tingling, which is not encoded by the pain rating. Zero pain does not mean clearance. No safe zone is shown. This chart is retrospective: the flat-ground zero includes follow-up confirmed after checkpoint 2. At checkpoint 2, that next-morning response is still unknown and cannot be replaced with this later value.
response.alt: Separate exposure and discomfort series for six selected episodes: 30 and 0; 36 and 0; 44 and 3 with tingling; 32 and 0 after review; 50 and 0; 62 and 0 for one restricted outing.
response.measureDescription: Exposure: documented throws. Response: maximum reported medial discomfort, 0–10.
