brief: Mateo is a fictional 24-year-old professional right fielder who throws right-handed and bats left-handed: the same shoulder throws and leads the swing. Gradually increasing discomfort developed during a dense game schedule without a traumatic event. The treating physician and physical therapist established a working diagnosis of rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain and chose nonoperative care. The case supplies this diagnosis; a graph or imaging phrase cannot establish it.

You coordinate permitted preparation and field exposure. The clinician owns medical reassessment and participation permission; coaches design baseball tasks within those limits. Convert “throwing feels good” into the role demonstrated, the unanswered question, and the next evidence needed. A roster opening supplies no missing capacity evidence.

All details and doses are synthetic teaching assumptions. Checkpoints occur after the clinical decisions described; correct answers do not accelerate healing. A postoperative shoulder, recurrent instability, or another diagnosis requires a different pathway and cannot inherit this nonoperative plan.

athlete.Age / level: 24 years / professional affiliate outfielder; synthetic athlete
athlete.Medical pathway: Clinician-established working diagnosis of rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain; nonoperative rehabilitation
athlete.Target role: Right field and batting across the intended game schedule, including reactive throws and recovery between appearances
athlete.Current status: Completed initial rehabilitation; clinician reviewing entry to controlled throwing
athlete.Your job: Coordinate permitted doses, expose missing role demands, document actual work, and brief the decision owners

constraints: Only the clinical team can expand medical participation permission. Coach or roster pressure cannot override it.

The agreed case instruction is to stop the throwing task and contact the clinician for new sharp/deep pain, a giving-way episode, new neurological symptoms, or a material loss of function. A number alone does not define these events.
Log warm-up and unplanned throws, batting work, intended task and effort, actual response, and the next agreed check. Unknown observations stay unknown.
No universal 90% symmetry rule, calendar date, pain cutoff, or successful session can independently clear unrestricted baseball.
Specific numbers in this case describe staff-approved fictional exposures. Do not copy them into a real athlete's program.

mnemonic.expansion: Role demands → Observed capacity → Limits and response → Evidence for the next step.

checkpoints.title: 1. Permission must name the task
story: Mateo reports comfortable daily activities. The clinician documents usable, nonpainful motion for the proposed task, improved measured capacity under the same test setup, and tolerated advanced rehabilitation drills. The current written permission is controlled catch, with no reactive defense or full batting practice. An older MRI report mentions superior labral signal; the treating physician has not identified that finding as the symptom generator.

observations.label: Clinical review
observations.interpretation: Permission has a defined scope; it is not permission for unrestricted fielding.

observations.label: Athlete report
observations.value: Comfortable with the planned catch task
observations.interpretation: Useful confidence information for this task, not a tissue-healing measurement.

observations.label: Imaging
observations.interpretation: Requires clinical correlation; do not replace the treating team's diagnosis with an image label.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What should you do before the first field session?

options.text: Use a postoperative SLAP protocol because the MRI mentions the labrum.
options.feedback: No procedure occurred. Imaging alone does not establish the symptomatic diagnosis.
options.consequence: Introduces unsupported restrictions and a false pathway.

options.text: Confirm the catch task, dose, stop instructions, recording owner, and response check.
options.feedback: Correct. Make permission implementable; ask Mateo to explain the limits back.
options.consequence: Produces interpretable exposure and response evidence.

options.text: Use comfortable daily life to justify full pregame throwing and batting.
options.feedback: Daily activities do not sample urgent throws or combined baseball work.
options.consequence: Introduces unprepared demands outside permission.

checkpoints.rationale: Start with clinical permission and operational clarity. The plan should specify the activity being tested, not merely say 'return to throwing.'
checkpoints.staffOwner: Treating clinician approves the task; rehab performance staff implements and records; Mateo reports experience.
progressionEvidence: Current clinical permission and relevant examination documented
Task, intended effort, total throws, rest, and response checks agreed
Player and field staff can repeat the same limits
stopOrReview: New or changed symptoms outside the agreed response
Unclear diagnosis, permission, or responsibility

checkpoints.title: 2. Change the question, not everything
story: Two separate controlled sessions each contain 24 total throws, including warm-up. Mateo reports no symptoms during either session or at the agreed following-morning check. The clinician now permits a small, preplanned outfield approach-and-throw component. The coach proposes increasing distance, throw count, urgency, and batting volume on the same day.

observations.label: Established exposure
observations.value: 24 controlled throws on each of two occasions
observations.interpretation: Repeat tolerance of the defined catch task has been demonstrated.

observations.label: New question
observations.interpretation: A relevant new demand can be sampled without pretending it equals reactive game defense.

observations.label: Batting
observations.interpretation: The lead shoulder's batting exposure remains a separate part of the day's record.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: Which next session best produces interpretable information within permission?

options.text: Double throws, extend distance, and add live batting.
options.feedback: Prior comfort does not establish tolerance of every new variable together.
options.consequence: Obscures the reason for a changed response.

options.text: Repeat stationary catch indefinitely despite permission to progress.
options.feedback: Repetition can resolve uncertainty, but here it leaves a known role gap unexplored.
options.consequence: Adds catch evidence without fielding evidence.

options.text: Substitute a small number of permitted approach throws while keeping other exposures stable.
options.feedback: Correct. Agree exact dose with the clinician and coach; interpretability matters more than a rigid one-variable rule.
options.consequence: Tests a clearly described fielding addition.

checkpoints.rationale: Progression should resolve a specific missing demand. Count, distance, intent, body position, rest, and batting context describe different dimensions.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Clinician defines permission; field coach designs the drill; performance staff reconciles the day's combined work.
progressionEvidence: Planned versus actual task recorded
Response to the new movement and subsequent recovery reviewed
Relevant confidence and movement quality described
stopOrReview: Player changes effort or adds work beyond permission
Response differs materially from the previous exposure

checkpoints.title: 3. The log reveals the missing exposure
story: The record first says '24 throws completed.' Mateo then explains that he added 12 hard relay throws with teammates and replaced his 20 tee swings with 40 live batting-practice swings. The following morning he reports 4/10 shoulder pain, stiffness, and a new sense of difficulty lifting the arm. These are changes from his prior response, not an acceptable-response threshold supplied by the course.

observations.label: Actual throwing
observations.interpretation: Actual count was 50% above the planned count; this arithmetic is not a tissue-load or injury-risk estimate.

observations.label: Actual batting
observations.value: 40 live swings rather than 20 tee swings
observations.interpretation: Both amount and task changed; the combined exposure prevents simple attribution.

observations.label: Next-morning report
observations.value: 4/10 pain plus stiffness and altered function
observations.interpretation: The qualitative change matters; do not treat 4 as a universal stop line.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What is the next professional action?

options.text: Pause throwing progression, correct the exposure log, and obtain clinical reassessment.
options.feedback: Correct. Record without blame. The clinician updates examination, restrictions, and permitted activity.
options.consequence: Uses the actual session and changed function.

options.text: Repeat 36 throws to test whether he can adapt.
options.feedback: Performance staff should not investigate a new functional complaint with a throwing challenge.
options.consequence: Adds exposure before resolving the clinical question.

options.text: Diagnose a new labral tear because pain followed hard throws.
options.feedback: Chronology and symptom intensity do not identify tissue pathology; batting also changed.
options.consequence: Turns a reassessment need into an unsupported diagnosis.

checkpoints.rationale: A setback changes the information available. Do not erase unplanned work, assign automatic causality, or advance by calendar despite altered function.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Clinician reassesses and updates permission; performance staff supplies the corrected log and informs field staff.
progressionEvidence: Clinical review completed and documented
Updated permissible activity understood by all staff
Subsequent response to the revised task established before further advancement
stopOrReview: New weakness, instability sensation, neurological symptoms, or worsening function
Persistent or recurrent response inconsistent with the clinical plan

checkpoints.title: 4. A perfect ratio can hide a problem
story: After reassessment and a revised period of rehabilitation, Mateo resumes clinician-approved catch and tolerates it. Standardized external-rotation force at the same test position is now 90 N on each side. Earlier in rehabilitation it was 90 N on the involved right side and 100 N on the left. A comparable pre-symptom right-side record was 112 N. The staff has not established the measurement error for these observations.

observations.label: Symmetry
observations.interpretation: The ratio improved because the reference value fell; the involved value did not rise.

observations.label: Within-athlete comparison
observations.interpretation: A 19.6% lower observed value warrants context and repeatable assessment; it is not a proven biological deficit of exactly that size.

observations.label: Role evidence
observations.value: Reactive deep-field throws not yet sampled
observations.interpretation: An isolated force test cannot fill the task-exposure gap.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: How should the return meeting interpret the 100% result?

options.text: Clear unrestricted right field because 100% exceeds a 90% standard.
options.feedback: Neither percentage is a universal baseball clearance threshold. Raw values, dominance, and demands matter.
options.consequence: Hides the denominator change and missing exposure.

options.text: Declare a cuff tear because force is below baseline.
options.feedback: Force output is not a tissue diagnosis; method, effort, symptoms, and conditioning affect it.
options.consequence: Converts a capacity concern into an unsupported diagnosis.

options.text: Report raw values, baseline, method limits, and remaining field demands.
options.feedback: Correct. Review comparable repeat assessment if indicated; the ratio is one observation.
options.consequence: Shows what improved, what did not, and what remains unknown.

checkpoints.rationale: Interpret the numerator and denominator before the percentage. Force measurements and throwing tolerance are complementary observations with different limits.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Clinician and sports scientist interpret the standardized test; rehab performance staff connects it to the permitted field demand.
progressionEvidence: Comparable method and raw values visible
Clinical assessment addresses the capacity concern
Proposed task matched to current permission rather than a ratio
stopOrReview: Pain, altered effort, or changed test setup makes comparison questionable
Capacity or function changes unexpectedly

checkpoints.title: 5. One shoulder has two baseball jobs
story: Later clinical review supports graded combined practice. Mateo has separately tolerated planned fielding throws and batting progressions. He still hesitates on a rushed crow-hop throw after sprinting to a ball. The coach suggests a full live session with unrestricted throws and batting because each isolated activity has gone well.

observations.label: Fielding
observations.interpretation: Reactive direction, urgency, and imperfect positioning remain additional demands.

observations.label: Batting
observations.interpretation: Separate tolerance does not automatically establish same-day combined tolerance.

observations.label: Confidence
observations.interpretation: Clarify the specific task and symptoms; neither dismiss the concern nor diagnose from it.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: Which practice design best addresses the remaining question?

options.text: Remove batting permanently to reduce the shoulder to one job.
options.feedback: The target role includes batting; temporary clinical modification differs from abandoning that demand.
options.consequence: Leaves a required game task unprepared.

options.text: Agree a bounded combined session with graded reactive fielding and permitted batting.
options.feedback: Correct. Record urgency, throws, batting, confidence, symptoms, and the next response check.
options.consequence: Samples the combination while retaining the unresolved task.

options.text: Use unrestricted scrimmage to let competitive instinct resolve hesitation.
options.feedback: Competition changes behavior but cannot replace preparation or permission.
options.consequence: Loses control of the exposure being evaluated.

checkpoints.rationale: A right-handed thrower who bats left-handed uses the right shoulder in two distinct roles. Integration should include the actual combination, not assume that two separate successes are interchangeable with it.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Clinician approves combined participation; outfield and hitting coaches coordinate tasks; performance staff reconciles exposures.
progressionEvidence: Relevant throwing positions and intent sampled within permission
Combined batting and fielding response recorded
Specific hesitation explored with the athlete and clinician
stopOrReview: Unexpected pain, loss of function, or instability sensation
A drill exceeds the approved urgency, volume, or task scope

checkpoints.title: 6. Practice success needs a receiving plan
story: Mateo completes repeated permitted practices, including combined batting and reactive defense, with stable clinical findings and agreed follow-up responses. The clinician authorizes a limited competitive appearance after the multidisciplinary review. A different staff group will receive him at the affiliate tomorrow; the manager asks simply whether he is 'active.'

observations.label: Permission
observations.interpretation: The permitted role and limits must travel with the player.

observations.label: Practice evidence
observations.interpretation: Supports the clinical decision but does not promise a symptom-free entire season.

observations.label: Operational gap
observations.value: Receiving staff has no detailed handoff
observations.interpretation: A sound plan can fail if warm-up, batting, defensive scope, and review responsibility are unclear.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What should the affiliate receive before the player is listed?

options.text: Send a task-specific brief with authorization, limits, exposure history, and receiving owners.
options.feedback: Correct. Include warm-up, batting, defense, response checks, and contingencies if game demands exceed the plan.
options.consequence: Makes participation limits executable and reviewable.

options.text: Send a green status because everyone understands active.
options.feedback: Roster eligibility and unrestricted physical capacity are different meanings of that word.
options.consequence: Allows ambiguity to create unplanned workload.

options.text: Send a throw-count ceiling with no batting or field-role information.
options.feedback: Count alone omits urgency, preparation, other tasks, and follow-up.
options.consequence: Leaves important exposures and responsibilities unassigned.

checkpoints.rationale: Return preparation includes operations. The clinical decision, the manager's use of the player, and the athlete's understanding must describe the same next milestone.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Sending and receiving clinicians confirm permission; manager and performance staff confirm implementation; one named person collects follow-up.
progressionEvidence: Receiving staff acknowledges the same restrictions
Actual competitive and preparation exposures captured
Postgame and next agreed response checks assigned
stopOrReview: Game circumstances cannot respect the permitted role
New clinical concern or unplanned exposure requires review

checkpoints.title: 7. Appearing in games is not the entire destination
story: Mateo progresses through clinically approved appearances. He completes three games with no reported symptoms and stable following-morning checks. He is making routine plays, but has had few deep-field throwing opportunities. The planned target is everyday right field; his current schedule still alternates appearances and recovery days. The front office asks whether he has returned to previous performance.

observations.label: Established
observations.interpretation: Participation and response under that schedule are documented.

observations.label: Opportunity gap
observations.interpretation: No opportunity is not the same as failure, but it also is not observed capability under that demand.

observations.label: Schedule gap
observations.interpretation: The proposed role adds repeatability and recovery demands beyond alternating appearances.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: Which report most accurately supports the next decision?

options.text: Fully restored: three symptom-free games establish the prior role.
options.feedback: The observed schedule and opportunities are narrower than the target.
options.consequence: Extends the conclusion beyond the evidence.

options.text: Failed return: few deep-field throws prove incapacity.
options.feedback: Limited opportunity is not a failed performance test.
options.consequence: Misclassifies missing evidence as a negative result.

options.text: Report successful participation, remaining gaps, and the next permitted exposure and review.
options.feedback: Correct. Integrate task execution, confidence, clinical status, and recovery. One statistic cannot establish shoulder recovery.
options.consequence: Advances the role while keeping uncertainty visible.

checkpoints.rationale: Return to performance concerns effectiveness and repeatability in the intended role. A game appearance, a symptom report, and a sport outcome answer related but different questions.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Multidisciplinary staff and athlete review the intended role; clinician owns medical scope and coaches evaluate baseball execution.
progressionEvidence: Relevant game or controlled-task opportunities identified
Response across the intended appearance schedule documented
Comparable baseball execution and athlete confidence reviewed with context
stopOrReview: Clinical response changes as schedule demands increase
Performance decline or hesitation prompts a specific question rather than a diagnosis from statistics

assignment.brief: Prepare a one-page receiving-staff brief and a two-session decision plan for Mateo after checkpoint 5. The clinician has permitted graded combined practice, not unrestricted games. Use the case evidence without inventing a medical permission or a universal target dose.
deliverables: A demand matrix covering controlled throwing, reactive outfield throwing, batting plus fielding, and repeated-day response; identify established evidence, gaps, and reviewer.
Two session questions with dose dimensions to agree, actual-work fields, response checks, and contingent hold/review actions.
The corrected setback arithmetic and why 50% more throws and 100% symmetry are not injury-risk or clearance calculations.
A 90-second staff handoff and brief player explanation.
rubric: Specifies task, intent, count, batting, and schedule rather than only “throwing tolerated.”
Preserves permission, names the clinician, and routes changed function for reassessment.
Reports 36 throws, 50% above plan, unchanged involved force, and measurement limits accurately.
Provides an executable task, actual-work record, follow-up, and decision owner.
Addresses urgent-throw hesitation without dismissing it or letting roster pressure fill a gap.
modelResponse: Mateo has permission for graded combined practice. Controlled throwing and separately progressed batting are established; the rushed crow-hop throw remains a confidence and exposure question. Agree the next task and exact dose with the clinician and coaches before execution.

Session A examines a permitted approach-to-throw progression combined with the allowed batting work. Log warm-up and task throws, effort/task changes, batting, symptoms, confidence, modifications, and following-morning function. Session B addresses the next uncertainty only after response review and appropriate permission—perhaps reactive variability or a relevant repeat-day pattern. Completion alone does not trigger advancement.

The setback involved 36 throws: 12/24 × 100 = 50% above plan, with batting also changed. This does not quantify injury risk. Force symmetry improved because the reference side fell; involved force stayed at 90 N. The 22/112 × 100 = 19.6% observed baseline difference needs measurement and clinical context.

Player explanation: “Your comfortable catch and batting are progress. We are checking the combination and the rushed throw you are unsure about. Tell us about all work, including extras. Changed symptoms mean reviewing the next step with the clinician; they do not mean you failed rehabilitation.”

recall.prompt: Without the diagrams, use ROLE to explain why 100% symmetry, one good catch session, and a game appearance answer different questions.
recall.answer: Role describes the full task and schedule. Observations establish isolated force or tolerance of a named exposure. Limits include denominator changes, untested reactive/combined demands, and repeatability. Evidence for the next step combines clinical review, actual task exposure, subsequent response, confidence, and the appropriate decision owner.

transfer.prompt: A left-handed pitcher has a repaired shoulder and reaches the same force values. Can he use Mateo's next session? Explain what changes.
transfer.answer: No. A repair introduces procedure-specific tissue-healing constraints and surgeon/rehabilitation permissions; the current nonoperative pathway cannot establish those. Pitching also requires a different task analysis, including mound demands and the intended pitcher role. Transfer the documentation and evidence questions, then rebuild the actual progression from that athlete's clinical plan and sport demands.

anatomy.title: One right shoulder, two baseball jobs
anatomy.caption: Original orientation schematic: the cuff surrounds the glenohumeral joint; the scapula provides the socket. Mateo’s right shoulder throws and leads his left-handed swing. This shows task overlap, not a pain generator or verified attachment footprint.
anatomy.alt: Conceptual scapula and upper humerus with a blue cuff envelope. Task arrows connect the region to throwing and batting. The right shoulder throws and leads this left-handed hitter’s swing; no pain generator or attachment footprint is identified.

sourceRefs.locator: Phase 2: Glenohumeral joint musculature; Scapular Stabilizers
The throwing motion; Posterior shoulder instability

demands.title: The outfielder's role is more than catch
demands.caption: Original role map. Each added task changes the question; the arrows organize a clinical discussion, not a mandatory dose ladder. Combined and repeated exposure need their own evidence.
demands.alt: Five illustrated demands progress from controlled catch to approach and throw, reactive fielding, combined batting and defense, and repeated game days.

steps.label: Controlled catch
steps.detail: Known task, effort, count, and response

steps.label: Approach + throw
steps.detail: Gathering steps and planned field position

steps.label: Reactive defense
steps.detail: Ball flight, urgency, and imperfect positions

steps.label: Repeat the role
steps.detail: Execution and recovery across the schedule

sourceRefs.locator: Phase 4 – Return to Throwing Phase; Return to Play
Return to Participation Process and Criteria; Table 1

response.title: Count and response tell different parts of the story
response.caption: Synthetic observations on selected, nonconsecutive days. Plot throws and next-morning pain separately with distinct units. Batting also changed on the 36-throw day. This is not a dose-response equation, pain threshold, diagnosis, or safe-count rule. Intervening clinical review and rehabilitation are omitted.
response.alt: Selected synthetic sessions record 24, 24, 36, 24, 30, and 42 total throws. Next-morning reported pain is respectively 0, 0, 4, 0, 0, and 0 out of 10. The third exposure includes unplanned hard throws and changed batting; later sessions occur after clinical review.

sourceRefs.locator: Phase 4 – Return to Throwing Phase: communication and symptom response
Return to Participation Process and Criteria

response.measureDescription: Exposure: total throws; response: following-morning self-reported shoulder pain, 0–10

title: The center fielder who can jog but cannot yet play
subtitle: Rebuild speed, braking, baseball decisions, and repeated game tolerance after a hamstring strain.
role: Rehab S&C coach with the athletic trainer, physical therapist, team physician, sport scientist, and field staff

sourceNotes.locator: Clinical Examination; Progressive Running; Eccentric Hamstring Exercises; Hip-Extensor Strengthening
sourceNotes.application: Combines clinical review, progressive running, and complementary strength work. Baseball tasks are original applications.
sourceNotes.limit: Narrative clinical review, primarily other running and field sports. No baseball-specific dose or clearance threshold is validated here.

sourceNotes.locator: Implementation Considerations; Outcome Measures; Can We Assess The Reinjury Risk at Return to Sport?
sourceNotes.application: Uses symptoms, apprehension, raw strength, task exposure, recovery, and shared decisions instead of one clearance score.
sourceNotes.limit: Associations and practical guidance do not predict an individual reinjury. Fictional measurements are case facts, not norms.

sourceNotes.locator: Background: Anatomy; Clinical Presentation, Physical Examination, and Differential Diagnosis; Postoperative Rehabilitation
sourceNotes.application: Explains the short-head exception and why proximal avulsion or a surgical repair requires a different pathway.
sourceNotes.limit: Authors describe variable protocols and preferred practices. Their postoperative dates and cutoffs are not adopted.

brief: You support a 25-year-old professional center fielder, Alex Rivera, who stopped while accelerating out of the batter’s box with left posterior-thigh pain. The treating clinician has established a sprint-related biceps femoris long-head musculotendinous strain; assessment has excluded proximal avulsion and other causes requiring a different pathway. These are supplied case facts, not diagnoses you infer from the mechanism.

The player wants to return for an approaching road series. Your job is to execute the authorized physical-preparation plan, describe what has actually been demonstrated, and identify what remains untested. The clinician owns diagnosis, restrictions, reassessment, and medical clearance. The player, performance team, and field staff contribute to the participation decision.

Each checkpoint supplies a later case state after the team’s prior review. Selecting a sound answer does not independently authorize the real-world progression. All measurements and schedules are fictional. Session numbers, symptom ratings, and velocity values are observations for reasoning; they are not a published protocol or a universal safety boundary.

athlete.Player: Alex Rivera — fictional professional center fielder
athlete.Injury: Clinician-established left biceps femoris long-head musculotendinous strain; nonoperative pathway
athlete.Role demands: Explosive starts, long pursuits, curved base running, braking, reactive direction changes, and repeated play after time standing
athlete.Reference data: Healthy-season speed and strength records exist using the same measurement methods
athlete.Current restriction: Only clinician-authorized running and strength tasks; no unrestricted competition

constraints: The calendar creates pressure but does not establish readiness.
Test methods, shoes, surface, start type, and measurement equipment must accompany comparisons.
A short home-to-first run does not document exposure to every longer outfield pursuit.
Symptoms, strength, confidence, field tasks, and the following-day response must be interpreted together.
The receiving affiliate needs the actual completed work, restrictions, unresolved gaps, and a named decision owner.

mnemonic.expansion: Build capacity • Add speed • Sample baseball demands • Evaluate repeated response

checkpoints.title: 1. Earn the first running exposure
story: Alex walks normally and reports little discomfort, but fast running has not been tested. The clinician has reviewed gait, localized symptoms, range of motion, and tolerated strength work and permits a supervised introduction to controlled running. The general manager asks whether comfortable walking means the player is nearly game-ready.

observations.label: Walking
observations.interpretation: Useful clinical context; it does not reproduce sprint demands.

observations.label: Strength work
observations.value: Short-range knee-flexor and hip-extensor tasks tolerated
observations.interpretation: A starting capacity sample, not proof of long-length or high-speed capacity.

observations.label: Permission
observations.interpretation: Permission is task-specific and must be documented.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What is the best next action?

options.text: Run a timed maximal home-to-first effort to establish readiness.
options.feedback: A maximal effort is outside the stated permission and adds an unprepared demand. Walking tolerance cannot establish sprint readiness.
options.consequence: Do not start this exposure; return to the authorized plan.

options.text: Begin the authorized controlled running, document the response, and retain strength work.
options.feedback: This respects the assessment and starts rebuilding the missing task. Record what was completed and review symptoms, movement, and recovery before changing it.
options.consequence: Advance only to a reviewed controlled-running session.

options.text: Wait until every strength value exactly matches the other leg.
options.feedback: Perfect symmetry is not an established prerequisite for all rehabilitation exercise. The uninjured side may also change, and the clinician has already authorized a bounded introduction.
options.consequence: Reassess the reason for delay with the clinician instead of inventing a new gate.

checkpoints.rationale: Separate clinical eligibility from competitive readiness. A permitted small exposure can produce useful information without pretending that ordinary walking or a single strength result clears the whole sport.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Treating clinician sets permission; rehab S&C coach delivers and logs the session.
progressionEvidence: Document authorized task, dose, surface, and symptom-monitoring instructions.
Record movement quality and the athlete’s confidence during and after running.
Arrange the next review and preserve the current restrictions.
stopOrReview: Stop the running task for new sharp pain, altered gait, or a changed symptom pattern and seek clinical review.
New proximal pain, marked bruising, weakness, or neurological symptoms requires reassessment, not a coaching diagnosis.

checkpoints.title: 2. A comfortable jog leaves several gaps
story: Alex tolerates the prescribed linear running and controlled starts. He wants to add a chase drill because he feels normal. Today’s session has a known speed ceiling and a generous stopping area; neither longer acceleration nor rapid braking has been assessed.

observations.label: Completed work
observations.value: 140 m of monitored running in the example session
observations.interpretation: Distance describes quantity; it does not specify peak speed or tissue loading.

observations.label: Following morning
observations.interpretation: Reassuring alongside the examination, but not an automatic progression rule.

observations.label: Untested tasks
observations.value: Faster running, short stopping zones, reactive pursuit
observations.interpretation: These require separate planned exposures.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: How should the next session change?

options.text: Progress one authorized running demand while keeping the others familiar.
options.feedback: The team can interpret the response more clearly if speed or exposure changes without simultaneously adding sharp stops, turns, and competition. Retain adequate space to decelerate.
options.consequence: Review the completed exposure before another increase.

options.text: Add reactive chase drills, repeated sprints, and hard stops together.
options.feedback: This stacks several untested demands. If symptoms change, the team cannot confidently attribute the response to one component.
options.consequence: Reduce the proposed change and obtain a specific plan.

options.text: Replace running with Nordic strength because it targets the injured region.
options.feedback: Strength work has value, but an exercise cannot demonstrate tolerance to the running and baseball tasks that remain absent.
options.consequence: Keep complementary strength and running rather than treating one as a substitute.

checkpoints.rationale: Control is an information tool. The aim is a deliberate return to demanding movement, not permanent protection from it. Speed, distance, rest, direction, and stopping requirements are separate planning variables.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Rehab S&C coach proposes the exposure; clinician confirms it fits current restrictions.
progressionEvidence: Record both completed distance and observed speed; do not infer one from the other.
Confirm tolerance during the task, afterward, and at the agreed follow-up.
Maintain knee-flexor and hip-extensor work with scheduling that considers fatigue.
stopOrReview: Do not use a pain score alone to justify simultaneous changes.
Unexpected stiffness, altered stride, or loss of confidence prompts review before increasing demand.

checkpoints.title: 3. Similar strength is not the finish line
story: Several controlled progressions have been tolerated. The current assessment supports introducing faster running. Alex’s bilateral knee-flexor results look symmetrical, but both are below his healthy reference. Field staff suggest clearance because the symmetry number looks good.

observations.label: Same-method strength
observations.interpretation: Approximately 98% symmetry; both are below earlier values of 340 N and 345 N.

observations.label: Observed speed
observations.value: 7.3 m/s in a long, controlled run
observations.interpretation: His comparable healthy reference is 8.8 m/s. These are fictional observations, not universal targets.

observations.label: Player report
observations.value: Comfortable linear running; hesitant when asked to chase
observations.interpretation: Apprehension identifies an unresolved task and a conversation, not dishonesty.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What best addresses the remaining gap?

options.text: Clear unrestricted play because symmetry exceeds 95%.
options.feedback: No such case clearance rule was established. The ratio hides bilateral change and does not demonstrate faster running, braking, or game tolerance.
options.consequence: Return to raw values and the untested demand list.

options.text: Stop all field work until every laboratory value reaches its historical maximum.
options.feedback: That replaces judgment with another unsupported absolute rule. Testing history informs the plan, while authorized field exposure can build and evaluate capacity.
options.consequence: Discuss the deficit and planned exposure with the clinical team.

options.text: Continue authorized speed exposure and strength development, while reviewing confidence and response.
options.feedback: This addresses the real task gap and the raw strength trend. Measure actual speed using comparable conditions; shorter effort or perceived effort alone cannot prove top-speed exposure.
options.consequence: Add higher-speed work under the agreed supervision and review.

checkpoints.rationale: A ratio can improve because the other leg worsens. Use raw force, comparable history, examination, running exposure, and confidence together. The 8.8 m/s reference helps describe this player’s demands; reaching it once would still not prove readiness for repeated games.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Sport scientist checks comparability; clinician and rehab S&C coach integrate the evidence.
progressionEvidence: Report raw values and the testing setup alongside symmetry.
Document achieved speed and the space available for acceleration and deceleration.
Ask which exact movement creates apprehension and practice it within permission.
stopOrReview: Review any change in pain, stride, or confidence before increasing intensity.
Do not label a velocity or force measurement as tissue healing.

checkpoints.title: 4. Respond to the setback without guessing
story: A later session combines faster running with newly introduced curved paths and additional repetitions. During the final effort Alex reports a new focal pull and stops. The next morning symptoms are 3/10 rather than his recent 0/10. He can walk, and an important game is approaching.

observations.label: Session change
observations.value: Speed, path, and repetition count changed together
observations.interpretation: Several plausible contributors changed; the log cannot identify causation.

observations.label: During the effort
observations.interpretation: This is a changed presentation needing assessment.

observations.label: Next morning
observations.interpretation: A meaningful case change; the number is not a universal injury threshold.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the same workout to determine whether the symptom is real.
options.feedback: Provoking another maximal exposure is not a diagnostic test for performance staff. A player can walk despite a problem that matters at speed.
options.consequence: Stop further provocative field work and notify the clinician.

options.text: Hold the provocative progression, report the details, and obtain clinical reassessment.
options.feedback: Document when the symptom occurred, actual work, next-day change, and any functional loss. The clinician decides whether the pathway or restrictions need revision.
options.consequence: Return only to tasks explicitly permitted after review.

options.text: Assume the strain has torn again and restart a fixed multiweek protocol.
options.feedback: The symptom warrants review, but it does not establish a diagnosis or a required calendar. The medical evaluation determines the implications.
options.consequence: Avoid a diagnosis based on the training log alone.

checkpoints.rationale: Respond to changed symptoms before arguing about readiness. Neither normalization nor catastrophizing is justified. The next checkpoint assumes reassessment has found no new condition requiring a different pathway and has authorized a revised progression.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Athletic trainer or physical therapist coordinates prompt review with the team physician as indicated.
progressionEvidence: Send the completed rather than planned exposure and the point when symptoms changed.
Record the clinician’s updated restrictions and the next review trigger.
Reintroduce previously tolerated tasks only when authorized.
stopOrReview: Do not continue sprinting through a new focal symptom to meet a roster deadline.
New neurological symptoms or marked proximal pain, swelling, or functional loss merits prompt clinical evaluation.

checkpoints.title: 5. Turn linear speed into baseball capability
story: After reassessment and a revised progression, Alex again tolerates the authorized strength and faster linear running. Planned turns and braking have been introduced successfully. The next task is to test baseball decisions without immediately reproducing the full uncertainty and density of competition.

observations.label: Demonstrated
observations.value: Repeated linear runs and planned stopping
observations.interpretation: Useful prerequisites; a predetermined endpoint differs from reacting to a ball.

observations.label: Still incomplete
observations.value: First-step reads, curved routes, baserunning turns, repeated fielding
observations.interpretation: Create a visible task list instead of calling all running equivalent.

observations.label: Player perspective
observations.value: Confident on planned routes; uncertain about a late direction change
observations.interpretation: Use a staged task, clear stop option, and feedback.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: How should baseball uncertainty be introduced?

options.text: Use bounded reactive tasks, then expand space, choices, and repetition after review.
options.feedback: Start with a limited read and known stopping area, then add realistic choices. Track accelerations, longer pursuits, turns, and braking separately.
options.consequence: Progress toward a representative practice sample.

options.text: Use an unrestricted live scrimmage as the first reactive exposure.
options.feedback: That adds uncertain routes, maximal intent, repeated plays, and competitive pressure together. It hides which demands were actually demonstrated.
options.consequence: Create intermediate exposures with explicit boundaries.

options.text: Use hitting only because fielding involves too much running.
options.feedback: Hitting can be one permitted activity, but it leaves the center-field and baserunning requirements unresolved. It cannot stand in for those tasks.
options.consequence: Retain a separate fielding and baserunning progression.

checkpoints.rationale: A baseball task is a movement plus information. A fly-ball read, a rounded base, and a late stop impose different demands from a straight timed run. These task examples are applied reasoning from broader rehabilitation evidence, not a validated baseball clearance battery.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Rehab S&C coach and field coach design the tasks; clinician confirms boundaries.
progressionEvidence: Demonstrate acceleration, longer pursuit, braking, turning, and role-specific decisions.
Record what was omitted or limited, including reaction choices and recovery between efforts.
Review next-day response and confidence before adding density.
stopOrReview: Hold the next addition if movement changes or the athlete cannot execute the task within the agreed limits.
New symptoms return the case to the medical review route.

checkpoints.title: 6. Specify what game entry means
story: Alex has completed representative practice and repeated field tasks with an acceptable response under the team’s individualized plan. The clinician considers limited game participation medically appropriate. A coach proposes designated hitter duties, describing them as almost no hamstring exposure.

observations.label: Permission
observations.interpretation: The team still needs an operational plan and a substitute.

observations.label: DH demand
observations.value: No outfield work; live baserunning remains
observations.interpretation: A ground ball can still demand an unplanned maximal acceleration.

observations.label: Game uncertainty
observations.value: Innings do not fix sprint count or route demands
observations.interpretation: A low planned workload does not guarantee low actual exposure.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What must the entry plan include?

options.text: Describe DH as a low-risk clearance test and let performance determine the limit.
options.feedback: DH reduces defensive exposure but cannot remove running demands. It is neither a medical test nor an automatic safe option.
options.consequence: Define actual permissions and contingency plans.

options.text: Clear every role because a representative practice was tolerated.
options.feedback: Practice supports a decision; it does not make role and density restrictions unnecessary. The supplied clinical permission is limited.
options.consequence: Keep the entry within the approved role.

options.text: Specify role, expected exposure, removal triggers, backup player, and next-day review.
options.feedback: The player and all staff need the same limits. Do not rely on an instruction to avoid hard running in a live play; if required tasks are not permitted, choose another participation plan.
options.consequence: Enter only the agreed role and audit the actual demands afterward.

checkpoints.rationale: Return to participation is a managed exposure. The clinician, athlete, and staff agree on acceptable uncertainty, communicate the plan, and retain the ability to stop or substitute. A box score alone cannot describe the rehabilitation dose.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Team physician or designated clinician owns medical clearance; manager implements the agreed role.
progressionEvidence: Communicate the permitted role, restrictions, removal triggers, and who can revise the plan.
Capture warm-up, game, and additional conditioning exposures.
Schedule a next-day clinical and performance review.
stopOrReview: If game demands cannot fit restrictions, revise the role before participation.
Symptoms or a changed movement pattern trigger removal and clinical review according to the agreed plan.

checkpoints.title: 7. A return date is not restored performance
story: Alex completes the first game without symptoms. During subsequent exposure, the staff notices fewer aggressive routes and a slower repeat sprint late in the session. He says he is protecting the leg when tired. The affiliate receiving him asks whether the rehabilitation file can be closed.

observations.label: Participation
observations.interpretation: This records an event, not sustained performance.

observations.label: Repeated demand
observations.value: Later-effort performance and confidence remain variable
observations.interpretation: Interpret the context; do not label the pattern as reinjury from data alone.

observations.label: Ongoing work
observations.value: Strength, running exposure, recovery, and communication still needed
observations.interpretation: Preserve the development plan through the handoff.

checkpoints.decisionPrompt: What is the strongest handoff decision?

options.text: Close the case because pain is zero and a game was completed.
options.feedback: This discards the performance and confidence gaps that the staff has observed. Pain alone does not establish role restoration.
options.consequence: Keep a documented return-to-performance plan active.

options.text: Transfer the demonstrated capabilities, remaining gaps, maintenance work, and review plan.
options.feedback: Separate medical availability from the performance tasks still being rebuilt. Agree on repeated exposure and criteria for follow-up without inventing a universal game count.
options.consequence: Receiving staff continue the agreed plan and report response.

options.text: Declare recurrent injury because a later sprint was slower.
options.feedback: Fatigue, pacing, measurement variation, or apprehension may contribute. Performance change is a reason to investigate context, not diagnose tissue damage.
options.consequence: Discuss the observation with the player and clinical team.

checkpoints.rationale: The endpoint is sustainable execution of the player’s role with an informed management plan. Continue complementary strength and running preparation rather than removing rehabilitation work as soon as games resume. The receiving staff must know both what passed and what remains uncertain.
checkpoints.staffOwner: Receiving athletic trainer and S&C coach acknowledge the handoff; clinical decisions remain with the medical team.
progressionEvidence: Review repeated game and practice demands, recovery, confidence, and comparable performance measures.
Continue individualized strength exposure while accounting for the game schedule.
Assign a named owner and date for the next follow-up.
stopOrReview: New focal symptoms or functional loss return to clinical review.
A decline in performance prompts context and measurement review before a medical conclusion.

assignment.brief: Write the affiliate handoff and propose the next two reviewed field exposures. Use the case facts; do not invent medical permission or a universal clearance threshold.
deliverables: A task matrix covering acceleration, longer high-speed pursuit, braking, turning, baserunning, reactive fielding, and repeated game demand. Mark demonstrated, limited, or not yet tested.
Two proposed field sessions showing the one main demand you would change, what stays stable, the response you will collect, and who must authorize the change.
A 150-word staff handoff with actual completed work, current restrictions, outstanding gaps, symptom-review triggers, and named receiving owners.
An explanation of why approximately 98% symmetry and 0/10 symptoms cannot independently establish readiness.
rubric: Clinical scope: distinguishes established diagnosis, task permission, medical clearance, and performance planning.
Specificity: treats speed, acceleration, braking, turning, reactive decisions, and repetition as distinct demands.
Interpretation: uses raw values and comparable history, and labels uncertainty without diagnosing from a chart.
Operations: describes completed work, follow-up response, escalation, and a receiving owner clearly.
modelResponse: The task matrix must show the changing evidence across the case. Early linear running supports neither reactive center-field work nor repeated game tolerance. By game entry, practice has sampled those demands, but sustained performance and fatigue-related confidence still need follow-up. Marking a task demonstrated should name the conditions rather than imply unlimited capacity.

For the next reviewed field exposure, preserve the already tolerated speed and task types while sampling a familiar reactive route pattern. If the clinical and next-day review supports it, a subsequent session can change the density of repeated role-specific efforts while keeping the main route and speed demands familiar. Actual repetitions and rest are agreed with the team from the player’s completed work; the case does not supply a validated prescription.

Example handoff: Alex has medical permission for the agreed limited role and has completed the recorded field and game exposures. Current concerns are confidence and repeat-effort execution when fatigued. Continue the authorized strength and running plan. Document actual warm-up, game, and additional field demands. Do not infer tolerance from innings alone. New focal symptoms, altered gait, or functional loss require clinical review before progression. The receiving athletic trainer owns symptom follow-up; the S&C coach owns exposure recording; field staff implement the agreed participation limits. Review together before adding game density.

Left/right force is 300/305 × 100 = 98.4%, but the left is still below its recorded 340 N reference and the right is below 345 N. Symmetry obscures those changes. Neither the ratio nor the historical value can replace clinical findings, demonstrated tasks, confidence, and repeated response.

recall.prompt: Hide the illustrations. Explain BASE and name three demands a comfortable jog does not establish.
recall.answer: Build capacity, Add speed, Sample baseball demands, Evaluate repeated response. A jog does not establish maximal-intent acceleration, higher-speed pursuit, rapid braking, reactive turning, or tolerance to repeated game demands.

transfer.prompt: Another player has a clinician-confirmed proximal tendon avulsion treated surgically. Can you copy this progression because both athletes have hamstring pain?
transfer.answer: No. The repaired tissue, surgical procedure, protection requirements, weight-bearing and range restrictions, and treating surgeon’s plan determine early rehabilitation. Obtain the operative details and explicit permissions. The shared principle is to build toward actual baseball demands with reviewed responses; this strain case supplies no postoperative dates or permissions.

anatomy.title: The hamstrings link hip and knee
anatomy.caption: Original schematic: the long hamstring units cross the hip and knee; the biceps femoris short head does not cross the hip. This case involves the long-head musculotendinous region, not a surgically repaired pelvic attachment. Location is conceptual, not an imaging diagnosis.
anatomy.alt: Conceptual pelvis, thigh and bent knee. A long blue posterior-thigh band represents the long hamstring group spanning hip and knee. A shorter band represents the biceps femoris short head crossing only the knee. These are grouped functional relationships, not individual attachment footprints.

response.title: Read the exposure together with the response
response.caption: Fictional monitored sessions, not seven consecutive days or a prescription. Distance is completed running, including controlled work; it is not a speed dose or tissue-load estimate. The zero is a known no-running review session. Symptom ratings show a case change, not a universal stop threshold. The setback followed several simultaneous task changes; this plot cannot establish causation.
response.alt: Seven session observations plot completed running meters alongside next-morning symptom ratings; symptoms rise after the mixed-demand session and lead to clinical review before a revised progression.
